title: Algorithm Problems
summary: Solve it on paper first. Then the Java is mostly typing.
refresher: Reading the problem is not the same as understanding it. Read it again, explain it out loud in plain language, then trace one tiny case by hand with a pencil. The thing you kept erasing and rewriting on that paper is the **variable** your program needs. Four shapes cover most first-year problems: a running total, a tally of how many, a best-so-far **value**, and a hunt for one matching item. All four are the same skeleton. Declare the variable above the **loop**, change it inside the loop, use it below the loop. Java is strict about the first of those. A variable declared between the loop braces is gone once the loop ends, and the compiler will stop the build rather than let you read it.

sections.title: Read and trace first
sections.summary: Say the problem back and work a small example by hand.

blocks.body: When a problem defeats you, the issue is often the plan, not Java. Slow down before typing. Read the prompt, choose what value you need to keep, and then write code from that plan.

blocks.title: Do these four things before you type
items: Read it twice. Write down what you are given and what you owe back.
Explain it to the wall in plain language. If the wall would be confused, so are you.
Trace one tiny case with a pencil. Three items, and show every step.
Study your own paper. The shape you just used has a name.

sections.title: Move from paper to code
sections.summary: Turn the hand trace into setup, loop, update, and return.

blocks.body: Start on paper first. If the task is to add 4, 8, and 15, write 0, then 4, then 12, then 27. You kept one running **value** and updated it for each number. That is the algorithm before Java gets involved.

blocks.caption: Your paper transfers almost line for line. `total` is the one number you kept going, the **loop** is the **values** arriving one at a time, and the **print** is you reading your final scribble aloud. From here on, examples drop the `public

sections.title: Recognize common patterns
sections.summary: Choose accumulator, counter, search, max, min, or index state.

blocks.body: Programmers call this an accumulator. Declare it above the **loop**, grow it inside the loop, read it below the loop. Three cousins of it will handle nearly every problem your first two semesters throw at you, and each one reuses those exact three moves.

blocks.title: The four shapes worth recognizing on sight
items: Accumulator: sums the **values**. Begin at 0, and grow it by each item.
Counter: answers how many. Begin at 0, and grow it by 1 whenever an `if` says yes.
Max or min: holds the champion. Begin with item zero, and swap when beaten.
Search: finds one match. Record where it was, then quit looking.

blocks.caption: Compare this to the accumulator above. Only two things moved: the `if` filters which items qualify, and the update grows by 1 rather than by the **value**. That tiny edit turns "what do they add up to" into "how many of them passed".

The champion starts out as item zero, and gets dethroned whenever the **loop** meets something larger. Beginning at 0 instead of `temps[0]` would quietly ruin this: every reading here is below freezing, so no **value** could ever unseat 0, and the program would report 0 as the warmest day.

blocks.title: temps[0] blows up on an empty array
blocks.body: If an **array** may be empty, check its length before reading slot 0. Java can compile `temps[0]`, but the program will crash at runtime if the array has no items. Use a guard such as `temps.length > 0` first.

blocks.caption: This task needs the position, so it uses `i`. Starting `found` at -1 means "not found yet" because no real index is -1. The `break` matters too: it stops at the first match instead of letting a later match replace it.

blocks.title: Two questions place every line for you
blocks.body: Ask two questions: What value am I keeping? What makes it change? The kept value becomes a **variable** above the **loop**. The change rule usually becomes an `if` inside the loop. Then return or print the variable after the loop.

sections.title: Order the lines carefully
sections.summary: Place setup, loop updates, builds, casts, and return in the right positions.

blocks.prompt: The task: "An **array** holds the rainfall for four days. On how many days did it rain at all?" Which shape solves it, and what does that shape **print** here?
blocks.code:
int[] rain = {0, 3, 0, 7};
// which shape belongs here?
choices: An accumulator adding up the rainfall. It prints 10.
A max tracker holding the wettest day. It prints 7.
A search that quits on the first rainy day. It prints 1.
blocks.why: "On how many days" is a tally, and a tally is a counter: begin at 0, grow by 1 whenever `r > 0` holds. Two of the four days have rain, so the answer is 2. The accumulator is placed there to tempt you, because both shapes walk the same **array** and both look at the same numbers. What separates them is the size of the step. A counter steps by 1, so `days++` answers "how many days", which is 2. An accumulator steps by the **value**, so `mm += r` answers "how much rain", which is 10. Same **loop**, same array, and the update line is the only thing that decides which question you answered.

blocks.body: In Java, the declaration has to be in the right place. If a **variable** is declared inside loop braces, it disappears when that loop pass ends. A line below the loop cannot use it.

blocks.caption: Only one line moved, but the meaning changed. If `int total` is inside the braces, Java creates it for one loop pass and then removes it. The print line below the **loop** cannot see it, so Java reports `cannot find symbol`.

blocks.title: A build that fails is the kinder outcome
blocks.body: Java checks the whole **file** before it runs. That can feel strict, but it helps: a compile error gives you a file and line number before any wrong answer appears.

blocks.prompt: This is supposed to report the largest number. It builds, it runs, and it says 7. What went wrong?
choices: The line `biggest = 0;` lives between the braces, so every pass erases the previous winner
The `if` should test `>=` rather than `>`, so that ties are kept
The `System.out.println(biggest)` line belongs between the braces
You cannot find a maximum without sorting the array first
blocks.why: The declaration is above the **loop**, which is why this builds at all. The reset is not. `biggest` is flattened to 0 at the top of every pass, so each comparison is only ever this item against zero, never against the champion so far. The final pass **leaves** 7 sitting there, and 7 is what you see. Sorting is the trap, because sorting genuinely would hand you 30. It also throws away the algorithm you were asked to write and leaves the erasing line untouched, waiting to spoil whatever you build next. Remove that single line and the code is right.

blocks.title: Two ints divided give you back an int
blocks.body: If `sum` and `marks.length` are both `int`, Java uses whole-number division. `253 / 3` becomes 84, not 84.33. Convert one side first, such as `(double) sum / marks.length`, when the decimal matters.

sections.title: When you are stuck
sections.summary: Use the rescue checklist before guessing.

blocks.title: A rescue plan for when you are stuck
items: One sentence on the **input**. One sentence on the **output**. Written down, not in your head.
Pencil out the smallest case you can imagine. Three items will do.
Note what you kept revising as you went. That is the **variable**.
Give it a shape: a sum, a tally, a champion, or a target you are hunting.
Declare above the **loop**, revise inside the loop, read below the loop.
"Cannot find symbol" from the compiler means you declared it between the braces.
An answer that is always the final item means you are erasing the **variable** every pass.

algo-01.title: Accumulator line order
algo-01.body: This Parsons problem is the classic running-total shape. Find the line that creates the total, the line that repeats over each value, the indented update, and the final output line.
algo-01.notice: The total has to exist before the loop can add to it.
algo-01.mistake: Do not put the output or setup line where it would run once per item unless the prompt asks for every step.

algo-02.title: Counting-loop bounds
algo-02.body: This is still an accumulator, but the values come from a counting loop instead of an existing collection. Trace which numbers the loop will produce before placing the update line.
algo-02.notice: The loop should generate exactly 1, 2, and 3.
algo-02.mistake: Do not let the boundary include one extra value or skip the first value.

algo-03.title: Best-so-far tracker
algo-03.body: A largest-value algorithm starts with a real candidate, scans each value, and replaces the saved best only when the current value is better.
algo-03.notice: The comparison and replacement belong inside the loop, with the replacement nested inside the condition.
algo-03.mistake: Do not start from an arbitrary value if the collection already gives you a safe first candidate.
algo-03.example: best starts as the first item

parsons-count-matches-01.title: Counter with a condition
parsons-count-matches-01.body: This problem counts matching values, so the counter changes only when the rule is true. The loop visits every value; the condition decides which visits count.
parsons-count-matches-01.notice: The count update belongs inside the if block, not just inside the loop.
parsons-count-matches-01.mistake: Do not increment for every item when the prompt asks for only matching items.

algo-p1-05.title: Even-value counter
algo-p1-05.body: This is a counter pattern with an even-number test. Arrange the setup, scan, test, counted update, and final output as separate jobs.
algo-p1-05.notice: The modulo test decides whether the counter changes.
algo-p1-05.mistake: Do not add the even number itself when the prompt asks how many even values there are.

algo-p1-06.title: Smallest-so-far tracker
algo-p1-06.body: Finding the smallest mirrors finding the largest. Start with a real value, compare each new value, and replace the saved answer only when a smaller value appears.
algo-p1-06.notice: The final output waits until every value has had a chance to challenge the current smallest.
algo-p1-06.mistake: Do not reset the smallest value inside the loop.
algo-p1-06.example: current smallest changes only on a smaller value

algo-p1-07.title: Search flag
algo-p1-07.body: A search flag starts as false, scans the collection, and changes to true if the target appears. The report happens after the scan is complete.
algo-p1-07.notice: The flag update belongs inside the condition that recognizes the target.
algo-p1-07.mistake: Do not print the flag before the loop has checked all values.

algo-p1-08.title: Countdown progress
algo-p1-08.body: A countdown loop needs an initial value, a condition that stays true while counting, an output step, and a progress step that moves toward stopping.
algo-p1-08.notice: The value must change inside the loop so the condition eventually becomes false.
algo-p1-08.mistake: Do not leave the decrement outside the loop body.
